:::{#thm-mgf-moments}
#### Moments from the moment generating function

If $M_X(t)$ is defined at every $t$ in some
[open interval](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets.html#def-open-interval) around $0$,
then for every [positive integer](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/number-systems.html#def-positive-integer) $k$,
the $k$-th [raw moment](#def-moment) of $X$ is the $k$-th
[derivative](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-derivatives.html#def-derivative) of $M_X$ at $0$:

$$\E{X^k} = M_X^{(k)}(0)$$

:::

::: proof

Let $h > 0$ be such that $M_X(t)$ is defined for every $\abs{t} < h$.
For any such $t$, the [series](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-infinite-sum)
of the [exponential](random-variables.qmd#def-exponential) gives:

$$\ef{tX} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k X^k}{k!}$$

The [absolute value](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-basics.html#def-absolute-value) of each summand
is at most the matching summand of $\ef{\abs{tX}}$.
Also, $\ef{\abs{tX}} \le \ef{tX} + \ef{-tX}$,
and $M_X(t)$ and $M_X(-t)$ are both defined,
so $\E{\ef{\abs{tX}}} < \infty$.
This domination lets the [expectation](expectation.qmd#def-expectation) pass through the series,
by the [Fubini--Tonelli](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-double-integrals.html#thm-fubini-tonelli) exchange:

$$
\ba
M_X(t)
&= \E{\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k X^k}{k!}}
&& \text{(power series of the exponential)} \\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{t^k}{k!}\E{X^k}
&& \text{(pass the expectation through the sum; linearity of expectation)}
\ea
$$

A [Taylor series](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-taylor-series.html#def-taylor-series)
can be differentiated one summand at a time
inside the [open interval](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets.html#def-open-interval) where it
[converges](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-taylor-series.html#def-taylor-series).
The $k$-th [derivative](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-derivatives.html#def-derivative) at $0$ keeps only the summand with $t^k$,
and that summand's coefficient is multiplied by $k!$.
So $M_X^{(k)}(0) = k! \cd \frac{\E{X^k}}{k!} = \E{X^k}$.

:::
